title: The lopsided Ganesha
hook: a clay Ganesha made by hand, a little lopsided, and the worry that it isn't good enough
tomorrow: Navaratri: nine nights of the Goddess

segments.voice: Yesterday: the butter thief, honored as God. Close enough to scold. Today, another small god, and a kitchen table covered in clay.

It's the week before Ganesh Chaturthi. Someone sits at the kitchen table with a lump of natural clay, because clay goes back to the earth when the festival ends. Two hours later there's a Ganesha. His trunk leans to one side. One ear is bigger than the other. The belly is great, though. Then they scroll past photos of other people's Ganeshas, smooth, painted, perfect, and the feeling turns. Embarrassed. A little jealous. Then guilty for being jealous. Someone online asked exactly this: am I a bad devotee? The answers came back warm. Today, the one people kept repeating.
screen: `A CLAY GANESHA, MADE BY HAND.` → `THE TRUNK LEANS.` → `AM I A BAD DEVOTEE?`

segments.voice: Start with the word for the figure itself: murti. It means a form, a body, a shape given to something. A murti isn't just a picture of God. Many Hindus understand it as a form God can be present in, and in many homes a short rite invites that presence before the worship begins. Temple murtis are often carved by trained craftsmen, following old rules for proportion. But look at what's honored at home. In many pujas, Ganesha is first called into a small cone of turmeric paste, or a single betel nut. No trunk. No ears. Shiva is widely worshiped as the lingam, a smooth rounded stone, and Vishnu as the shaligram, a dark stone from a riverbed in Nepal. Some of the most honored forms have no face at all. So what's being weighed? You met the verse on day eight. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that whoever offers him a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water with devotion, he accepts it. Nothing on that list is fine art. The love is the offering; the clay only carries it. And the jealousy? The people who answered said, gently, that feeling it is part of being a whole person, and noticing it is already something. Or, as people like to put it: Ganesha isn't an art critic. Like a parent with a child's drawing on the fridge, he sees who made it, and how. And a clay Ganesha that melts back into the water at the end of the festival? That isn't a flaw. That's the plan.
screen: `MURTI — A FORM, A BODY.` · `SOME HAVE NO FACE AT ALL.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · `NOT AN ART CRITIC.`

segments.voice: Picture something you made, a drawing, a meal, a message, a messy first try, flaws and all. Notice the voice that starts comparing it to someone else's; let it talk without arguing, then remember who made it, and why. If you pray, you can offer it, crooked edges and all; if you don't, just let it be enough for now.
Murti. A form, a body: the shape in which God is honored, from carved stone to a cone of turmeric. Today's word.
Your line: he's not an art critic. The love goes in first; the clay just carries it. On to day eighty-seven.

chat.says: My clay Ganesha came out lopsided. Is it still okay to worship it?
options: Yes. The love is the offering; the clay only carries it. He's not an art critic.
Only if it looks like the photos online; a crooked one can't hold his presence.
Only as decoration; a clay one made at home can't be used for a real puja.
